title: Snap one banana off a bunch without dragging the bunch or denting the fruit, and lay it in an open lunch box
instruction: Take one banana off the bunch and put it in the lunch box.
context: Packing a banana for lunch starts with taking one off the hand of bananas on the counter. A ripe banana's stem lets go when the banana is bent or twisted at its root (about 0.6 N m: about 5 N lifting it 14 cm out from the stem). Pulled on its own, the light bunch slides and turns along with it before the stem gives, so a careful person holds the bunch down by its crown with one hand and bends one banana up with the other. Only one banana may come off, the rest of the bunch should stay where it was, and the fruit is soft: a hard pinch dents it. The banana then goes in an open lunch box, lying inside below the rim, not perched on it. The hand of four lies curved side down; the outer bananas splay out from their neighbours, which leaves a finger's room beside them.
setup: Millimetres from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, heights above the table top. 1) Bananas: a hand of four ripe Cavendish bananas (for example Chiquita), colour stage 6 (all yellow, no green tips, no brown flecks), joined by their stems to the crown (the cut cushion of the bunch, about 90 x 32 x 50, brown, about 150 g, estimate). Each banana about 195 along its outer curve (USDA medium: 7 to 7 7/8 in), 36 thick at the middle, 150 g (estimates within the published medium range), stem about 15 thick; the four stems leave the crown's front face about 22 apart at x = 95, 118, 140, 162, y = 124, 33 up. The bananas lie curved side down, rolled about 35 degrees so the inner curve faces up and toward +x, heading toward -y and fanned 24 and 5 degrees toward -x and 6 and 18 degrees toward +x (the outer banana toward -x is the one nearest the right arm); the crown is centred at (130, 140). Peel friction about 0.7 (estimate). 2) Lunch box: a Sistema Lunch 2 L rectangular box (maker: 235 x 170 x 80 closed, 212 g with lid), clear polypropylene plastic base, open, centred at (270, -215) with its long side along y; base about 70 deep, walls 3, 150 g (estimates). Its blue plastic lid (about 62 g, estimate) lies flat, top up, beyond it at (465, -215). 3) The table is bare; the pads wear thin nitrile glove covers (pad covers, so no peel residue builds up).
scoring: Judged at the end from the trial video, a photo and a ruler. Score 0 if: no banana has come off its stem; two or more have; a banana or the crown has fallen off the table; a banana still on the bunch has a dent deeper than 5 mm or a split skin; the detached banana's flesh is exposed. Otherwise exactly one banana is off and the score is the lowest of three numbers. Place: 1.0 the banana lies wholly inside the box, below the rim, let go and still; 0.5 it rests partly on or over the rim or wall, or is inside but still held; 0.25 it is anywhere else (on the table, still held outside the box). Damage to that banana: 1.0 no dent deeper than 5 mm and no split; 0.75 a split under 10 mm at the shoulder; 0.5 a split 10 to 20 mm or a dent 5 to 8 mm deep; 0.25 a longer split or a dent over 8 mm, flesh still covered. Crown moved from its start (tape mark round it, ruler from the mark): 1.0 up to 10 mm, 0.75 over 10 and up to 30 mm, 0.5 over 30 and up to 60 mm, 0.25 more; a crown turned more than 10 degrees about the vertical (protractor, its cut face against the tape line) scores at most 0.75. In simulation a dent is a pinch over 40 N held 0.2 s (5 to 8 mm) or at the gripper's 48 to 50 N limit (over 8 mm); the peel cannot split.
reset_notes: About 3 minutes. One fresh hand per trial; a hand is never used twice. Source: buy retail bunches of six to eight Cavendish bananas at colour stage 6, 1 to 2 days before, all from one shop display, and keep them at room temperature (20 to 22 C, at least 2 h out of any fridge; cold stems hold harder). With a kitchen knife cut straight down through the crown so that four neighbouring bananas stay joined on one crown piece about 90 mm long (the trial hand, as in the setup) and the other two to four stay on the other piece (the sample cluster); cutting the crown snaps no stem. Stem strength is sampled on the sample cluster only, never on the trial hand: hold the cluster's crown on the table, hook a kitchen scale round its outer banana 14 cm from the stem and lift until it snaps; use the trial hand if the scale read 300 to 800 g (3 to 8 N, 0.4 to 1.1 N m), else set that bunch aside. Reject a trial hand with a split skin, a torn crown or a dent over 5 mm. Lay the hand curved side down, all four bananas attached, with the crown on its tape mark at (130, 140). Empty and wipe the box, stand it at (270, -215), lid beyond it. Wipe the table; change the pad covers if sticky. After the trial the bananas are eaten. Cost about 3 dollars a bunch (one trial); box about 8 dollars.
fidelity: Rigid bodies. Each banana is one rigid body joined to a rigid crown by a fixed joint that PhysX breaks for good at 0.6 N m bending (estimate; real stems 0.4 to 1.2) or 80 N pull, so the stem lets go only when the banana is bent or twisted hard enough. The peel cannot split or bruise: a dent is read from the gripper's squeeze (over 40 N for 0.2 s). Banana shape: lofted convex pieces at true size. Box and lid are thin rigid shells.
